CausalChain: Hypoxia in HCC → HIF activation → Upregulation of LDHA and MCT4 → Increased lactate production and export → Extracellular lactate accumulation leads to acidification and engagement of receptors (e.g., GPR81) → Upregulation of PD-L1 and suppression of NK/CD8+ T cell function → Creation of an immunosuppressive TME → Drug resistance to TKIs and ICIs
Hypothesis: Inhibiting MCT4-mediated lactate export in hypoxic HCC will reduce lactate-induced immunosuppression, restore NK and CD8+ T cell cytotoxic function, and downregulate PD-L1 expression, thereby sensitizing tumors to immune checkpoint inhibitors and overcoming drug resistance.
Abstract: Hypoxia in hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) is well known to drive metabolic reprogramming through the activation of hypoxia‐inducible factors (HIFs). This reprogramming results in a switch to glycolytic metabolism, with concomitant upregulation of enzymes like lactate dehydrogenase A (LDHA) and lactate transporters such as monocarboxylate transporter 4 (MCT4). The accumulation of lactate in the tumor microenvironment (TME) contributes not only to the metabolic symbiosis between hypoxic and normoxic cancer cells but also to an immunosuppressive milieu by inducing PD‐L1 expression and impairing the function of cytotoxic lymphocytes, including NK cells and CD8+ T cells. Here, we propose that inhibiting lactate export through targeted blockade of MCT4 could alleviate lactate‐mediated immune evasion. When combined with agents that stimulate NK cell activity and with immune checkpoint inhibitors, this strategy may restore robust antitumor immunity and overcome inherent drug resistance observed in hypoxic HCC.
